newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Vietnam leads Asia invective against U.S. attacks.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam leads Asia invective against U.S. attacks.

text.p: Vietnam on Wednesday denounced its former enemy the United States for misplaced aggression, leading the official Asian invective in reaction to the U.S. missile attacks on Iraq.

Australia said Washington was tough but right, Taiwan gave its whole hearted support and Japan, the world's biggest importer of Middle East oil, called for a quick resolution to the most serious U.S.-Iraqi confrontation since the Gulf War.
The United States launched a second wave of cruise missiles against military targets in southern Iraq on Wednesday in retaliation for Iraqi military intervention in the country's Kurdish north.
"Vietnam is following the situation in this region with deep concern," a Vietnamese Foreign Ministry spokesman said in a statement.
"Regardless of the circumstance, to use force against a sovereign state is contrary to international law, is not in line with the common global trend, and is unacceptable," he added.
Vietnam, which fought the Americans in a drawn-out and bloody war that ended 21 years ago, was critical of the U.S.-led military campaign against Iraq in 1991.
Indonesia also expressed concern about "territorial integrity" and urged restraint by both sides.
"In this context, Indonesia reiterates its basic stand that the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Iraq should be respected," Foreign Minister Ali Alatas told reporters.
U.S. officials said 17 missiles were fired from four ships on Wednesday. The second wave was aimed at targets not destroyed in the attack by 27 missiles on Tuesday.
China was silent on Wednesday, but on Tuesday had expressed "grave concern" over the U.S. attack.

"We deeply regret new tensions arising in the Gulf," state radio quoted Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang as saying. "We have always been against resorting to military force or mutual threats to resolve international incidents."
Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer called the second U.S. cruise missile attack tough but right.

"It is tough action but it is tough action which we think is understandable and we support it," Downer told reporters. "Let us hope that (Iraqi President) Saddam Hussein understands the mistake he has made and that he begins to behave in a responsible way. It is in everybody's interest that he does."
Japan, a strong backer of U.S. action against Iraq, on Wednesday called for Baghdad to immediately withdraw its forces from Kurdish areas of the country.
Speaking minutes after the United States announced the second attack, deputy government spokesman Kazo Watanabe said the crisis could only be settled by an Iraqi withdrawal.
"Japan strongly hopes for Iraq to withdraw from the northern areas (of Iraq) in order to settle the situation at the earliest possible instant," Kazo told a news conference.
In comments earlier on Wednesday before the second U.S. attack, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he was concerned at the size of the forces Iraq was moving into Kurdish areas.

"Although I haven't actually seen everything on a satellite or anything, I am concerned that the Iraqis are moving thousands of military men and hundreds of tanks to the Kurdish area," Hashimoto said.
Taiwan was brief in its reaction but to the point.
"The Foreign Ministry thinks the U.S. government's action is justified and appropriate," it said in a statement.
